blocks.text: Rust eating through a zinc roof, a battery powering a torch, iron being smelted from its ore, food going stale — all four are the same piece of chemistry. Electrons are moving from one substance to another, and once you can track them, an enormous slice of chemistry falls into place.

blocks.markdown:
## Three ways to define it

The definition of oxidation has widened over time. All three versions are still examined.

| | Oxidation | Reduction |
|---|---|---|
| Oxygen | Gain of oxygen | Loss of oxygen |
| Hydrogen | Loss of hydrogen | Gain of hydrogen |
| Electrons | Loss of electrons | Gain of electrons |
| Oxidation number | Increase | Decrease |

The electron definition is the most general and the one to use when in doubt.

blocks.title: OIL RIG
blocks.text: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain — of electrons. Say it out loud once and you will not confuse the two again.

blocks.markdown:
### Redox reactions always happen together

Electrons cannot simply vanish. If one species loses electrons, another must gain exactly the same number at the same moment. That is why the combined process is called a **redox** reaction.

Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) -> Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s)

Split it into half equations:

- Oxidation: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-
- Reduction: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu

Zinc loses two electrons and the copper ion gains exactly those two.

blocks.title: Oxidising and reducing agents
blocks.text: An oxidising agent oxidises another substance, which means it takes electrons and is itself reduced. A reducing agent reduces another substance, which means it donates electrons and is itself oxidised. The agent always undergoes the opposite change to the one it causes.

blocks.title: Identifying the agents
blocks.prompt: In the reaction H2S + Cl2 -> 2HCl + S, identify what is oxidised, what is reduced, and name the oxidising and reducing agents.

steps.text: Track the hydrogen. H2S loses its hydrogen to become S, and loss of hydrogen is oxidation, so hydrogen sulphide is oxidised to sulphur.
Track the chlorine. Cl2 gains hydrogen to become HCl, and gain of hydrogen is reduction, so chlorine is reduced.
Confirm with oxidation numbers. Sulphur goes from -2 in H2S to 0 in S, an increase, confirming oxidation.
Chlorine goes from 0 in Cl2 to -1 in HCl, a decrease, confirming reduction.
Now name the agents. Chlorine caused the oxidation of the sulphur, so chlorine is the oxidising agent, and it was itself reduced.
Hydrogen sulphide caused the reduction of the chlorine, so it is the reducing agent, and it was itself oxidised.

blocks.answer: Sulphur is oxidised and chlorine is reduced; chlorine is the oxidising agent and hydrogen sulphide is the reducing agent

blocks.title: Hydrogen peroxide can do either
blocks.text: Hydrogen peroxide usually acts as an oxidising agent, but against a stronger oxidising agent such as acidified potassium manganate(VII) it behaves as a reducing agent and releases oxygen. Always read the other reagent before deciding.

blocks.title: Say which species, not just which compound
blocks.text: When a question asks what is oxidised, name the actual species that lost electrons — 'the iron(II) ion' or 'the sulphide ion' — rather than the whole compound. Full marks are given for the precise species.

points: Oxidation is loss of electrons, gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen; reduction is the reverse.
Oxidation and reduction always occur together, since electrons lost by one species are gained by another.
An oxidising agent gains electrons and is itself reduced.
A reducing agent loses electrons and is itself oxidised.
Acidified potassium manganate(VII) and potassium dichromate(VI) are the standard oxidising agents, with clear colour changes.
